power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease associated with the destruction of cartilage and bone, increased risk of cardiovascular disease and a higher mortality rate.
Despite the many therapies that exist for RA, there is little information to guide selection of the most effective treatment for an individual patient.
Ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies have created an opportunity to investigate the target tissue.

While a number of studies have characterized the stromal and immune cell populations using single-cell technology on synovial biopsy samples, here we performed a longitudinal study, where we collected comprehensive clinical data over a one-year period on each patient in the process of changing their therapy.

Methods: Samples from minimally invasive, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were collected from RA patients at baseline prior to start of a new therapy and 4-6-week follow-up under IRBapproved protocols with informed consent.
Comprehensive clinical data from each appointment were recorded into a shared REDCap database.
Failure to respond to therapy was based on clinical disease activity index (CDAI) for RA after 12-18 weeks post therapy.

Biopsied samples were dissociated, enriched for CD45⁺ or CD45⁺CD11b⁺ cells, and processed on the 10X Genomics Chromium platform to generate libraries for single-cell RNA sequencing with cell-surface protein detection (CITE-seq).
Spatial transcriptomics were performed on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded sections analyzed with 10X Xenium and NanoString CosMx.
Results: We performed CITE-seq analysis on ~38,000 CD45+ synovial cells isolated from 17 patients who failed a conventional or biologic DMARD and planned to change therapy.

Prospective transcriptional studies, which include Pathobiology of Early Arthritis (PEAC) [15, 16], Rituximab Versus Tocilizumab in Anti-TNF Inadequate Responder Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis (R4RA) [17, 18], and Stratification of Biological Therapies for RA by Pathobiology (STRAP) [19, 20], demonstrated that histological scoring, and pathotype or endotype are not sufficient to predict therapeutic response to an individual therapy.

text.text: In this study, we performed a prospective longitudinal analysis of RA patients who were either naïve to any therapy or were switching therapy.

All patients underwent an ultrasound guided synovial biopsy at baseline, from which tissue was used for cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq) and/or spatial transcriptomics.
We observed that the proportion of macrophages were enriched in non-responders, while conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) were enriched in the responder populations.
We observed the ISG15 + and THBS1 + macrophage subpopulations were enriched in non-responders.
The ISG15 + macrophages were localized to the lining, while the THBS1 + cells may be found in the sublining.
These findings suggest that specific macrophage states in the synovium before treatment can predict subsequent 100 therapeutic response.

text.text: Prepared sample libraries were pooled, quality control (QC) by Tapestation performed by the Division of Rheumatology-Pulmonary and Critical Care Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) facility, and sequenced on an Illumina Novaseq machine.
Before full sequencing, MiniSeq runs were performed to ensure the quality of samples and to estimate cell number for more accurate sequencing depth.

Raw single-cell RNA-sequencing data generated on 21 patient samples (17 baseline, 4 follow-up) using the 10x Genomics platform were processed with Cell Ranger (v7.0.0) using the cellranger count pipeline.
Reads were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38-3.0.0 with includeintrons = false, and gene-by-cell UMI count matrices were generated.
Ambient RNA contamination was corrected using SoupX (v1.6.2).
All downstream analyses were performed in R using Seurat (v5.2.1).
Cells with mitochondrial transcript content greater than 15% were excluded, and putative doublets were identified and removed using DoubletFinder (v2.0.4).
Following quality-control filtering and doublet exclusion, a total of 37,459 high-quality cells were retained for downstream analyses (Supplemental Table 2).

text.text: RNA expression counts were normalized using SCTransform, with Seurat-derived S phase and G2/M phase cell cycle scores (S.Score and G2M.Score), computed from canonical cell cycle gene sets, regressed out during normalization.
A total of 3,000 highly variable genes identified by SCTransform were used for principal component analysis (PCA).
Sample integration was performed in PCA space using Harmony to correct for inter-sample technical variation.

The Harmony-corrected embeddings were subsequently used for UMAP visualization, nearest-neighbor graph construction, and graph-based clustering using the Seurat functions RunUMAP, FindNeighbors, and FindClusters, respectively.
The first 10 Harmony dimensions were used for downstream analyses, and clustering at a resolution of 0.1 identified 11 transcriptionally distinct clusters.
Clusters were labelled as myeloid, T cells, B cells, Plasma cells, or mast cells based on canonical markers.
For CITE-seq data, antibody-derived tag (ADT) counts were normalized independently for each sample using centered log-ratio normalization in Seurat (margin = 2).
ADT measurements were used for downstream protein-level visualization and to support cluster annotation.
Visualization shows log-normalized RNA expression counts.
De novo marker genes for each cluster were identified using the Seurat FindAllMarkers function with only.pos = TRUE and min.pct = 0.25 (Supplemental Tables 4 5).

text.text: For myeloid sub-clustering, cells corresponding to the myeloid compartment were first extracted from the full dataset.
To ensure robust annotations, we chose 5 representative samples containing more than 300 myeloid cells and having a median UMI count greater than 2000 as the reference set for myeloid sub-clustering.
RNA expression data were re-normalized using SCTransform for each sample individually, using the default number of 3,000 highly variable genes, and Harmony was used for integration.
The first 10 dimensions were used for downstream analysis, and clustering was performed at a resolution of 0.45.
Sub-cluster identities were assigned on the basis of canonical marker genes together with de novo cluster genes (defined as above).
Following annotation of the reference myeloid subset, subcluster labels were transferred to myeloid cells from all other samples using the Seurat reference-mapping workflow.

Briefly, myeloid cells from all samples were independently normalized using SCTransform and transfer anchors were identified between the annotated reference object and the query cells using Seurat's FindTransferAnchors with normalization.method = "SCT".
Predicted subcluster labels were then assigned using TransferData, and query cells were mapped onto the reference UMAP using MapQuery.
Associations between myeloid cell-type abundance and clinical response status were assessed using Mixed-effects modeling of Associations of Single Cells MASC (v0.1.0-alpha) [37].

text.text: For this analysis, only baseline samples were analyzed (responder = 12, non-responder = 4, 1 patient excluded due to lack of follow-up).
Only cell types represented by at least five cells in each comparison group (responder vs. non-responder) were retained.

A logistic mixed-effects model was fitted for each myeloid cell type, with response group included as the contrast of interest, age included as a fixed effect, and sample identity included as a random effect.
Likelihood ratio testing was used to assess the significance of the response term, and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated from the fitted models.
Adjusted p values were calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method.
Differential gene expression analysis was performed using a pseudobulk strategy with edgeR (v4.0.16) [38].
text.formatted: Differential gene expression analysis was performed using a pseudobulk strategy with edgeR (v4.0.16) <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>.

text.text: For each cell population of interest, raw RNA counts were aggregated at the sample level to generate pseudobulk expression profiles.
Only genes with non-zero expression in at least 50% of pseudobulk samples were retained for testing.
Normalization and robust dispersion estimation were performed using edgeR.
Differential expression between responders and nonresponders was then tested using generalized linear models and likelihood-ratio testing.
Genes were considered differentially expressed with P value < 0.05 and an absolute log2(fold change) > 0.5.
text.formatted: Genes were considered differentially expressed with P value < 0.05 and an absolute log2(fold change) > 0.5.

text.text: For visualization of individual genes, pseudobulk expression was scaled to counts per million (CPM).
Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed on the pseudobulk differential expression results using the fgsea package (v1.31.0) [39].
text.formatted: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed on the pseudobulk differential expression results using the fgsea package (v1.31.0) <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: All genes retained following filtering in the edgeR pseudobulk differential expression analysis were included in GSEA.
Genes were ranked using a composite statistic defined as -log10(raw P value) × log2(fold change), such that both statistical significance and effect size contributed to the ranking.
Hallmark gene sets, KEGG canonical pathways, and Reactome canonical pathways for Homo sapiens were obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) [40] using the msigdbr package (v7.5.1).

text.text: The fgsea algorithm was run with 20,000 permutations on gene sets with a minimum size of 5 genes and a maximum size of 1,000 genes.
Enrichment results were summarized using normalized enrichment scores (NES), nominal P values, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted P values.

For each differentially expressed gene from the baseline macrophage pseudobulk edgeR analysis, mean log-normalized RNA expression by subtype for each sample were averaged within responder and non-responder groups.

The resulting gene-by-group expression matrices were standardized by row using Z-scores and clustered separately by K-means based on increased (K = 4) or decreased (K = 3) expression and in responders vs. non-responders.
The number of clusters was selected based on the resulting expression patterns and biological interpretability of the gene groups.
Cluster-level expression profiles were summarized by calculating the mean Z-score across all genes in a cluster for each macrophage subcluster and response group.
Heatmaps and cluster profiles were generated using ComplexHeatmap and ggplot2, respectively.

The relative contribution of individual subtypes to macrophage expression was calculated as the counts from each subtype over the total macrophage counts for the given gene in each sample; these values were then averaged across samples within responder and non-responder groups.
The scaled contribution for each gene was calculated by multiplying the average subtype contribution by the average CPM across samples for each responder group.
Associations between myeloid cell proportions and clinical characteristics were assessed using 16 baseline RA synovial biopsy samples.

Associations with clinical variables, including treatment outcomes, demographics, serology, medication history, and baseline disease characteristics, were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for binary variables and Spearman's rank correlation for continuous variables.
Effect sizes for binary variables were calculated using rank-biserial correlation coefficients.
Adjusted p-values were calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method.
Associations were visualized using heatmaps displaying the corresponding effect sizes, with nominal significance indicated at p < 0.05.

text.text: Spatial transcriptomic data were generated as previously described [41] using one patient on the NanoString CosMx 1,000-gene panel and obtained from NanoString output files containing the gene-by-cell expression matrix and the corresponding cell-level metadata.
text.formatted: Spatial transcriptomic data were generated as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> using one patient on the NanoString CosMx 1,000-gene panel and obtained from NanoString output files containing the gene-by-cell expression matrix and the corresponding cell-level metadata.

text.text: Initial quality-control filtering was performed by retaining cells with total RNA counts between the 5th and 98th percentiles of the dataset.
For doublet identification, the filtered dataset was first processed using SCTransform, followed by DoubletFinder with pK optimization using paramSweep, summarizeSweep, and find.pK.
The expected number of doublets was adjusted for homotypic doublets using the modelHomotypic function.
Following doublet removal, cells were re-normalized using SCTransform, and variable features were identified.
Spatially informed clustering was then performed using BANKSY (v0.99.13).
Briefly, RunBanksy was applied to the normalized RNA assay using the cellular spatial coordinates with lambda = 0.2 and k_geom = 15.
Principal component analysis was then performed on the resultant BANKSY assay, which is a concatenation of the normalized gene expression matrix and a spatial neighborhood expression matrix.
Harmony integration was carried out at the field-of-view (FOV) level using RunHarmony on the BANKSY PCA embeddings to account for tissue sampling variability.
The Harmony-corrected BANKSY embeddings were subsequently used for UMAP generation (RunUMAP), nearest-neighbor graph construction (FindNeighbors), and graph-based clustering (FindClusters).
The first 11 principal components and a clustering resolution of 0.7 were selected for downstream analyses.
Cluster marker genes were identified using Seurat's FindAllMarkers function and interpreted together with canonical markers for major synovial cell populations.

Xenium spatial transcriptomic data were generated on 11 patients using a 196-gene panel (Supplemental Table 3) and were processed using Xenium Ranger, and the resulting output matrices were imported into R with mols.qv.threshold = 20.
text.formatted: Xenium spatial transcriptomic data were generated on 11 patients using a 196-gene panel (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">3</ref>) and were processed using Xenium Ranger, and the resulting output matrices were imported into R with mols.qv.threshold = 20.

text.text: To define spatially coherent tissue sections within each sample, density-based spatial clustering was performed independently for each sample using DBSCAN (eps = 100, minPts = 10) on the global x and y coordinates to identify individual tissue density clusters (TDC), roughly equating to pieces of tissue, for quality control.
For each TDC, the total number of cells and average cell density were calculated based on occupied 100 × 100 µm spatial tiles, with tile area converted from µm² to mm² for reporting cell density.
TDC were retained if they contained at least 100 cells and had a cell density of at least 500 cells/mm².
A second level of filtering was then applied at the individual cell level, and cells with fewer than 10 Xenium UMI counts (nCount_Xenium > 10) were excluded.
text.formatted: A second level of filtering was then applied at the individual cell level, and cells with fewer than 10 Xenium UMI counts (nCount_Xenium > 10) were excluded.

text.text: Each sample (including all TDCs passing QC) was independently normalized using SCTransform, with all 196 genes in the targeted Xenium panel retained as variable features.
Spatially informed clustering was performed using BANKSY with lambda = 0.2, M = 1, and k_geom = 15.
PCA was performed on the BANKSY assay using 30 principal components.
To account for sample-and section-specific technical variation, Harmony integration was performed using RunHarmony, grouped by spatial section and sample identifier.
Harmony-corrected BANKSY embeddings were subsequently used for UMAP generation and nearest-neighbor graph construction.
The first 20 Harmony dimensions were used for downstream analyses.
For cell-type annotation, the CosMx dataset was used as a reference for label transfer after restricting the reference to genes included in the Xenium 196-gene panel.

Transfer anchors were identified using FindTransferAnchors, and predicted labels were assigned to Xenium cells using TransferData, thereby projecting CosMx-derived annotations onto the Xenium dataset.
Spatial neighborhood analysis was performed using the CosMx label-transferred cell-type annotations.
To prevent artificial neighborhoods spanning independent tissue regions, neighborhood composition was calculated independently within each tissue-density cluster.
Within each tissue density cluster, the 20 nearest neighbors of every cell were identified from cell-centroid coordinates.
A neighborhood-composition profile was generated for each cell by counting the number of neighboring cells belonging to each annotated cell type.
Neighborhood-composition profiles from all tissue density cluster were subsequently combined into a single matrix.
Cells with similar neighborhood-composition profiles were grouped using mini-batch K-means clustering.

Multiple cluster numbers were evaluated, and five niches were retained based on the clarity and biological interpretability of cell-type-enriched neighborhood patterns. the cellular composition of each niche was summarized by averaging neighborhood-composition profiles across all cells assigned to the corresponding niche.
The resulting niche-level composition matrix was standardized by Z-score transformation and visualized using a scaled heatmap.

text.text: Here, we present a prospective, longitudinal study of RA patients who had ultrasoundguided synovial biopsies for single-cell RNA seq and for spatial transcriptomics, prior to change in therapy and monitored over time.
We observed that the proportion of total macrophages is reduced in RA patients who respond to therapy.
Further, we identified that ISG15 + and THBS1 + macrophage subpopulations correlate with response to therapy as indicated CDAI-20.
Moreover, the ISG15 + and THBS1 + populations appear to localize preferentially to the lining and sublining tissue, respectively.
This study is the first to link transcriptionally defined synovial macrophage subpopulations, profiled prospectively before a change in therapy, to subsequent therapeutic response.
